title: A cauldron of loves (Confessions 3.1)
hook: young Augustine in Carthage, in love with being in love
tomorrow: when a friend dies, what does everything you look at become?

segments.voice: That was a week of desert elders and one opening prayer: lifted hands, a bent bow, smoke before fire, demons who couldn't be humble, a mouth taught by the heart. Yesterday's line: restless until it rests in you.
screen: `SIX LINES FROM THE DESERT AND A PRAYER.` → `RESTLESS UNTIL IT RESTS IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Some playlists are all longing: songs about someone, with no someone yet. Augustine describes that from a big, loud city. Carthage, and a young man newly arrived. Looking back years later, the first thing he remembers is noise. All around him, he says, a cauldron of unholy loves was sizzling and singing. He isn't in love with anyone yet. He's in love with being in love.
screen: `SONGS WITH NO SOMEONE YET.` → `CARTHAGE, SIZZLING.` → `IN LOVE WITH BEING IN LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here is his line, in plain English: I did not love yet, and I loved to love; I went looking for something to love, in love with loving. No villain, no scandal named. Just a hunger without an object. Then he says what he thinks the hunger really was: a famine of inward food, and that food was God. He didn't feel hungry for that. He felt hungry for everything else. One for a friend tonight: some readers hear a pun in the Latin, where the city is Carthago and the cauldron is sartago, a frying pan. A city that sizzles. And the Confessions is still a prayer, spoken to God, so this isn't bragging about wild years or beating himself up. The point isn't that love is bad; Augustine spends the rest of the book on love. It's what yesterday's restless heart looks like from the inside.
screen: `I LOVED TO LOVE.` · `A FAMINE OF INWARD FOOD.` · `CARTHAGO, SARTAGO.` · `NOT AGAINST LOVE.` · then, large: `IN LOVE WITH LOVE.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and write one line by hand: something you're in love with right now, a person, a plan, a screen, a hope. Under it, write what hunger it might be feeding. Don't judge either line; just look at them for the rest of the sit.
A cauldron of loves. Augustine's picture of Carthage: a pot sizzling with loves, and a heart in love with love itself.
Your line: in love with love. A hunger still looking for its food. That's the week, done.

fork.setup: your cousin starts a new relationship the week the last one ends, and laughs, 'i just love love.' what would Augustine ask her?
options: so who's next on the list?
what are you really hungry for?
why not swear off dating for good?
fork.reveal: Augustine read his own hunger as a famine of inward food. he didn't scold the loving; he asked what it was for.

original.note: Latin: I loved to love. from Confessions 3.1, nondum amabam, et amare amabam: I did not love yet, and I loved to love.

chat.says: Caleb asked me to prom and i said yes instantly. do i like HIM or just being asked??
options: Fair question, not a crime. Name the hunger, then go find out who he is.
Just being asked. Wanting love is shallow; cancel before it gets worse.
Doesn't matter. Any love is love; Augustine says follow the feeling.
chat.meaning: Augustine doesn't call love bad. He names a hunger still looking for its food, and asks what it's really for.
